components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我在公园里看到了一只小狗。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài gōngyuán lǐ kàndào le yì zhī xiǎo gǒu.
example.english: I saw a little dog in the park.
example.fact: 看到 pairs the verb 看 ("to look") with the result complement 到 ("to arrive, to achieve") to mark that the looking actually succeeded in perceiving something. The same verb+到 achievement pattern reappears in 找到 (also in this batch, rank 70, "to find") — a productive template for turning a plain effort-verb into a success-verb.

components.note: Depicts a person standing tall, gazing up at the moon 月 — the image of looking into the distance, the source of 望's meaning 'to gaze, hope, expect.'

example.hanzi: 我希望明年能去中国旅行。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xīwàng míngnián néng qù Zhōngguó lǚxíng.
example.english: I hope I can travel to China next year.
example.fact: 希望 functions as both a verb ("to hope") and a noun ("a hope, a wish") with no change in form at all — the same free noun/verb flexibility the pilot batch’s 工作 entry (rank 43) describes, so 我的希望 ("my hope") and 我希望 ("I hope") reuse the identical word in two different grammatical roles.

components.note: 二 (two) — 些 originally suggested a small plural amount, building on the idea of 'more than one.'
此 (cǐ) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches the modern reading xiē.

example.hanzi: 那些照片是我去年拍的。
example.pinyin: Nàxiē zhàopiàn shì wǒ qùnián pāi de.
example.english: Those photos are ones I took last year.
example.fact: 那些 mirrors the pilot batch’s 这些 (rank 37) exactly, just swapping in the far-demonstrative 那 for the near-demonstrative 这 — together with 那样 and 那里 (both also in this batch), it shows the whole 那-family of words tracking one-for-one against its 这-family counterpart.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.pinyin: “Nǐ huì lái cānjiā jùhuì ma?” “Dāngrán huì!”
example.english: "Will you come to the party?" "Of course I will!"
example.fact: 当然 sits toward the confident end of Mandarin’s certainty spectrum — stronger than 也许 (also in this batch, "perhaps") and close in strength to 肯定 (also in this batch) — but 当然 specifically frames something as obvious or expected, rather than merely asserting that it’s true.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 许 relates to giving permission through words.
午 (wǔ) gives a hint of the sound — 许 is pronounced xǔ, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.pinyin: Tā yěxǔ yǐjīng dào jiā le.
example.english: He's perhaps already arrived home.
example.fact: 也许 is a near-synonym of 可能 ("maybe, possible") — 也许 leans a shade more literary and typically opens a clause as a sentence adverb, while 可能 moves more freely and can also stand in as a noun meaning "possibility," as the pilot batch’s own 可能 entry (rank 27) already notes.

components.note: 月, appearing twice side by side, originally depicted two people (or two strings of shells) together — giving 朋 its meaning 'friend, companion.'
又 (hand), shown twice and joined together — two hands clasped in friendship gave 友 its meaning 'friend.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zuì hǎo de péngyou.
example.english: He is my best friend.
example.fact: 朋 alone is already a pictograph of two people (or two strings of shells) side by side, and 友 separately pictures two hands clasped together — 朋友 doubles up two independently "companionship"-themed pictographs into one word, the same word-building strategy the pilot batch’s 喜欢 and 应该 entries use for fusing near-synonymous halves.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 妈 refers to one's mother
马 (mǎ) gives a sound close to 妈's reading mā, differing only in tone
女 (woman) — 妈 refers to one's mother
马 (mǎ) gives a sound close to 妈's reading mā, differing only in tone

example.hanzi: 妈妈每天早上都做早饭。
example.pinyin: Māma měitiān zǎoshang dōu zuò zǎofàn.
example.english: Mom makes breakfast every morning.
example.fact: 妈妈 is 妈 reduplicated with a toneless second syllable — the same doubling pattern behind 爸爸 (also in this batch) — and this kind of babyish reduplication for "mom/dad" recurs across unrelated language families (mama, papa), likely because doubled syllables are among the easiest sounds for infants to produce.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 相 pictures looking closely at a tree.
目 (eye) — staring closely at a tree to examine it gave 相 the meaning 'to observe' or, later, 'each other, mutual.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiāngxìn tā shuō de shì zhēn de.
example.english: I believe what he said is true.
example.fact: 相信 expresses trust or conviction that something is reliable or true, distinct from 认为 and 以为 (both also in this batch), which introduce a personal opinion or judgment rather than an act of trust — 相信他 ("to trust him") and 认为他对 ("to think he’s right") reach for different verbs even though English "believe" can cover both.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 认 relates to recognizing or acknowledging something, often expressed through words.
人 (rén) gives the sound — 认 is pronounced rèn, a close variant of the same sound.

example.hanzi: 大部分人都认为这是个好主意。
example.pinyin: Dàbùfen rén dōu rènwéi zhè shì gè hǎo zhǔyi.
example.english: Most people think this is a good idea.
example.fact: 认为 sits at the more formal, reasoned end of Mandarin’s "think" verbs — the pilot batch’s 觉得 entry (rank 23) already contrasts with it as the more common, subjective-feeling "think," while 认为 shows up disproportionately in writing, argument, and reporting rather than casual chat.

components.note: 儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.pinyin: Nǐ qù nàr, wǒ qù zhèr.
example.english: You go there, I'll go here.
example.fact: 这儿 attaches the colloquial "erhua" (儿化) suffix -r directly onto 这 — the same Beijing-flavored rhotacization the pilot batch’s 这里 entry (rank 17) already flags as a regional variant. 这儿/那儿 are the casual, spoken-register counterparts to 这里/那里 (also in this batch).

components.note: 亼 — traditionally linked to an image of gathering or covering; its original pictorial sense has become obscure, but the character came to mean 'now, the present.'
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.pinyin: Jīntiān tiānqì hěn hǎo.
example.english: The weather is nice today.
example.fact: 今 alone already carries the sense "now, the present" (the same root behind 现在 in the pilot batch, rank 10, and 如今), while 天 supplies "day" — 今天 combines them transparently into "the present day," the same logic behind 明天 ("tomorrow") and 昨天 ("yesterday").

components.note: 日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.
Originally depicted a burning candle or the sun's rays radiating outward — the source of 白's meaning 'white, bright, clear.'

example.hanzi: 老师讲了两次,我才明白。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī jiǎng le liǎng cì, wǒ cái míngbai.
example.english: The teacher explained it twice before I understood.
example.fact: 明白 marks a flash of comprehension — grasping how or why something works — while 知道 (pilot batch, rank 3) simply marks awareness that a fact exists. A speaker can 知道 a rule exists without yet being able to say they 明白 it, a distinction English’s single verb "to know/understand" doesn’t force you to make.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
十 (here a straight vertical line) — 直 pictures something drawn perfectly straight.
目 (eye) — looking directly and steadily with the eye gave 直 its meaning 'straight' or 'direct.'

example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí zài děng nǐ de diànhuà.
example.english: She has been waiting for your call the whole time.
example.fact: 一直 combines "one" with 直 ("straight") into an image of an unbroken straight line — the same 一 + [verb/adjective] pattern behind the pilot batch’s 一起 (一 + 起, "rise," rank 40) and this batch’s own 一切 and 一定. Extended metaphorically, it means an action or state continuing straight through without interruption, whether in time (一直等, "waiting the whole time") or space (一直走, "go straight ahead").

components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'
手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'

example.pinyin: Ràng wǒ kànkan zhè běn shū.
example.english: Let me take a look at this book.
example.fact: 看看 reduplicates the verb 看 with a neutral-tone second syllable — exactly the "soften a request" pattern the pilot batch’s 谢谢 entry (rank 21) already names 看看 as an example of. Repeating a one-syllable verb makes the action sound brief and casual, much like English "just take a quick look."

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè ānjìng de dìfang.
example.english: This is a quiet place.
example.fact: The pinyin here reflects the neutral-toned reading dìfang, the everyday word for "place, location" that actually explains this word’s top-100 frequency rank. Dictionaries also record a separate, fully-toned reading dìfāng, reserved for the narrower administrative sense "local, regional" (as opposed to 中央, "central") — the same one-hanzi-string, two-register-readings split as 告诉 in the earlier batch.

meanings: anyway (to get back to a previous topic)

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 这个包很贵,不过质量真的很好。
example.pinyin: Zhège bāo hěn guì, búguò zhìliàng zhēn de hěn hǎo.
example.english: This bag is expensive, but the quality is really good.
example.fact: 不过 is the softest, most casual member of Mandarin’s "but" trio, as the pilot batch’s 但是 entry (rank 18) already lays out: 但是 is neutral and standard, 可是 a shade more conversational, and 不过 the softest of the three — useful for gauging register when contrasting two ideas.

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 昨天晚上发生了一件奇怪的事。
example.pinyin: Zuótiān wǎnshang fāshēng le yí jiàn qíguài de shì.
example.english: A strange thing happened last night.
example.fact: 发生 is reserved for events, incidents, and changes of state — never for a person or object’s own physical arrival, which instead uses verbs like 到 or 来. Its second character 生 (also picturing new growth breaking out of the earth, as seen in the pilot batch’s 先生 entry, rank 25) frames an event as "growing into" existence.

components.note: 回 depicts a spiral or winding shape — something that turns back on itself, giving rise to the meaning 'to return.'
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ shénme shíhou huílai?
example.english: When are you coming back?
example.fact: 回来 anchors the "return" action toward the speaker’s own location — swap 来 ("toward here") for 去 ("toward there") and 回去 means "to go back" to somewhere else instead. The same toward-speaker/away-from-speaker contrast also distinguishes 出来 and 过来 (both also in this batch) from their 去-counterparts.

components.note: 冫 (water) — 准 originally referred to a carpenter's level using water to check flatness, extended to 'standard, accurate, level.'
隹 (zhuī) gives a sound hint — 准 is pronounced zhǔn, sharing the base sound though the vowel and tone differ somewhat.
夂 (to go) — heading out.
田 (farm field) — going out to the fields ahead of the harvest season, the act of preparation giving 备 its meaning 'to prepare, get ready.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhèngzài zhǔnbèi wǎnfàn.
example.english: We are preparing dinner right now.
example.fact: 准备 doubles as an auxiliary verb meaning "to be about to, to intend to" right before another verb (准备走了, "about to leave"), on top of its plainer sense "to prepare, get ready" — one of several Chinese verbs, alongside 要 and 打算, that slide from a full action verb into signaling near-future intention.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — represents an action performed by hand.
戈 (a spear/dagger-axe) — an old image of searching or probing with a weapon in hand, giving 找 its meaning 'to search, to look for.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我终于找到了我的钥匙。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zhōngyú zhǎodào le wǒ de yàoshi.
example.english: I finally found my keys.
example.fact: 找到 is built from the same verb+到 achievement pattern as 看到 (also in this batch, rank 51) — 找 alone only names the act of searching, and adding 到 confirms the search actually succeeded. Without it, 我找钥匙 just means "I’m looking for my keys," with no guarantee they turned up.

components.note: 父 (father) — 爸 names a father.
巴 (bā) gives a sound close to bà, sharing the same syllable body and differing only in tone.
父 (father) — 爸 names a father.
巴 (bā) gives a sound close to bà, sharing the same syllable body and differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Bàba zài kàn diànshì.
example.english: Dad is watching TV.
example.fact: 爸 shares a root with the more formal, literary word for "father," 父, while the doubled, neutral-toned 爸爸 is the affectionate, everyday form children actually use — roughly parallel to how English distinguishes the formal "father" from the everyday "dad/daddy."

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
刀 (knife) — relates directly to 切's meaning 'to cut.'
七 (qī) gives a sound hint — 切 is pronounced qiè, sharing the same initial consonant.

example.pinyin: Yíqiè dōu huì hǎo qǐlai de.
example.english: Everything will get better.
example.fact: 一切 combines "one" with 切 (built from 刀 "knife" + 七, its phonetic — literally "to cut") into an old image of "everything cut into one whole." Like the pilot batch’s 所有 entry (rank 48), it typically appears with 都 later in the sentence to land the "without exception" meaning on the verb, rather than carrying that force alone.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action is done with the arms.
包 (to wrap) — wrapping your arms around something gives 抱 its meaning 'to hold, to hug.'
欠 (lack) — 歉 describes a lack or shortfall, and later, the feeling of owing an apology.
兼 (jiān) gives a sound distantly related to 歉's reading qiàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Bàoqiàn, wǒ lái wǎn le.
example.english: Sorry, I'm late.
example.fact: 抱歉 sits a notch more formal than the everyday 对不起 (also in this batch) — common in announcements, customer service, and written apologies ("抱歉给您带来不便," "sorry for the inconvenience"), whereas 对不起 is the default spoken apology between friends and strangers alike.

components.note: 咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'
见 (to see, perceive) — relates to 觉's meaning 'to feel, sense, perceive.'
⺍ is a small graphic element serving as the phonetic hint, though its link to jué's modern sound has faded after centuries of change.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gǎnjué jīntiān tèbié lèi.
example.english: I feel especially tired today.
example.fact: 感觉 shares its second character with the pilot batch’s 觉得 (rank 23) — both use 觉, "to perceive" — but 感觉 leans toward physical sensations and gut impressions (累, 冷, 不舒服), while 觉得 more often introduces an opinion or judgment about something external, a subtle overlap that trips up learners reaching for "feel" in English.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the source of speech.
八 here suggests something small or simple leaving the mouth, giving 只 its meaning 'only, merely.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhǐshì xiǎng bāng nǐ yí gè máng.
example.english: I just wanted to help you out.
example.fact: 只是 often works less as a plain "merely" and more as a softening hedge right before explaining a real reason, especially at the start of a mild objection or excuse ("我只是...", "It’s just that I...") — much like English speakers reach for "I just..." to make a statement sound less confrontational.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 怎's meaning 'how' relates to a mental inquiry, what's on one's mind.
乍 (zhà) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zěn.
木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 这个周末去爬山,怎么样?
example.pinyin: Zhège zhōumò qù páshān, zěnmeyàng?
example.english: How about going hiking this weekend?
example.fact: 怎么样 extends the pilot batch’s 怎么 (rank 9) with the added suffix 样 ("appearance, kind"), and the pilot’s own 怎么 entry already flags the payoff: 怎么样 stands alone as a complete question about quality or status ("How is it?"), while bare 怎么 needs a following verb to ask "how" an action is done.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Tàiyáng chūlái le.
example.english: The sun has come out.
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense, 出来 works as a productive verb-complement suffix meaning "to emerge into being" (想出来, "to think up [an idea]") or "to manage to tell by looking" (看出来) — the same kind of layered, abstract extension piling onto a literal directional verb that the pilot batch’s 起来 entry (rank 35) describes.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.pinyin: Búyào chídào le!
example.english: Don't be late!
example.fact: 不要 is Mandarin’s standard prohibitive — negating the modal 要 ("must, will") with 不 to forbid an action — and it’s commonly clipped to just 别 in casual speech (别迟到, same meaning) — two completely different-looking words doing the identical job of "don’t."

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'
The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.

example.pinyin: Duìbuqǐ, wǒ bú shì gùyì de.
example.english: Sorry, I didn't mean to.
example.fact: 对不起’s pieces are often parsed as 对 ("to face") plus 不起 ("unable to manage," the same negative-potential pattern behind 买不起, "can’t afford," and 看不起, "to look down on") — a vivid folk-style breakdown of being too ashamed to face someone, now worn down into Mandarin’s default spoken "I’m sorry."

components.note: 亠 — read as the head of an animal standing upright in this pictograph; the character was later reused for the unrelated meaning 'to leave, be apart from, distance.'
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.pinyin: Tā zuótiān líkāi le Běijīng.
example.english: He left Beijing yesterday.
example.fact: 离开 takes its object directly, with no preposition needed (离开北京, "to leave Beijing") — a common trap for English speakers who instinctively want to insert "from," since 离 alone already carries the sense of separation "away from" built into the verb itself.

meanings: (used in negative expressions) (not) the least bit

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhǐ dǒng yìdiǎn Zhōngwén.
example.english: I only understand a little Chinese.
example.fact: 一点 attached after a noun or adjective softens a statement into "a bit of X" (有一点贵, "a little expensive") — but the negative form 一点都不 intensifies rather than softens, flipping into "not in the least" (一点都不贵, "not expensive at all"), a construction that surprises learners expecting the negation to simply cancel the "a little" meaning.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.pinyin: Míngtiān nǐ yídìng yào lái.
example.english: You must definitely come tomorrow.
example.fact: 一定 sits near the top of Mandarin’s certainty ladder alongside 肯定 (also in this batch) — but 一定 leans toward expressing a strong intention or requirement ("一定要," "must"), while 肯定 leans toward a confident assessment of fact ("肯定是," "it’s definitely [true that]"), a nuance easy to blur since English "definitely" covers both.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — relates to motion or progress.
不 (not) — 'not yet moving on' gave 还 its meaning of 'still, yet.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào hē chá háishi kāfēi?
example.english: Do you want to drink tea or coffee?
example.fact: 还是 does double duty as both "still" (还是老样子, "still the same as before") and the choice-question connector "or" (茶还是咖啡, "tea or coffee") — two meanings that look unrelated in English but share an underlying sense of "as before, among the alternatives already on the table."

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.hanzi: 科学家发现了一种新的病毒。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiā fāxiàn le yì zhǒng xīn de bìngdú.
example.english: Scientists discovered a new virus.
example.fact: 发现 combines 发 ("to bring forth") with 现, built from 见 ("to see") — literally "to bring into sight," a vivid image for discovery. It shares its first character with 发生 (also in this batch, "to happen"), two related but distinct extensions of 发’s core sense "to emit, set forth."

components.note: Originally a pictograph of a stone altar or ancestral tablet; its later use as the grammatical word 且, 'moreover, and,' has no connection to that original picture.

example.hanzi: 这家餐厅很便宜,而且很好吃。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng hěn piányi, érqiě hěn hǎochī.
example.english: This restaurant is cheap, and moreover it's delicious.
example.fact: 而且 typically completes a "不但...而且..." ("not only...but also...") frame when both halves of a sentence are explicitly marked, though in casual speech 不但 is often dropped while 而且 alone still carries the "and what’s more" sense on its own.

components.note: 彡 (hair) — growing hair.
页 (face/head) — hair growing on the face, originally 'beard, whiskers,' later extended to the abstract meaning of 须, 'must, necessary.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ bìxū xiān wánchéng zuòyè.
example.english: You must finish your homework first.
example.fact: 必须 marks a hard, often external obligation — a rule or requirement that isn’t optional — sitting at the strongest end of the want/need/must spectrum the pilot batch’s 需要 entry (rank 28) lays out, stronger than both 要 ("want") and 需要 ("need").

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
An altered form of 囟 (the mind/head) — the seat of thought.
心 (heart) — thinking was pictured as an activity of both mind and heart, giving 思 its meaning 'to think.'

example.pinyin: Zhège cí shì shénme yìsi?
example.english: What does this word mean?
example.fact: 意思 anchors two fixed phrases that both trip up learners: 有意思 means "interesting" (literally "has meaning/interest"), while 不好意思 means "excuse me, embarrassed" (literally "not good meaning") — neither English translation obviously has anything to do with "meaning," despite both being built directly from 意思.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
钅 (metal/gold) — represents something valuable.
昔 (formerly, in the past) — valuable metal that has been mishandled or lost over time gave 错 its meaning 'mistake, wrong.'

example.pinyin: Zhège zhǔyi búcuò.
example.english: This idea is not bad.
example.fact: 不错 literally negates 错 ("mistake, wrong") to get "not wrong" — but in everyday use it has drifted from a neutral "correct" into a mild positive compliment, "pretty good," the same kind of understated-praise shift English speakers make when they say something is "not bad" and mean it as a genuine compliment.

components.note: 止 depicts a foot coming to a stop.
⺼ (flesh, muscle) — pausing to make an effort willingly gave 肯 its meaning 'to be willing, to agree.'
宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.pinyin: Tā kěndìng zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He definitely knows about this matter.
example.fact: 肯定 can double as a verb meaning "to affirm, to give recognition to" (肯定他的努力, "to acknowledge his effort") on top of its more common adverbial sense "definitely, for sure" — two senses that share the same core idea of affirming something as real or worthy, whether that something is a fact or a person’s effort.

components.note: 电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
example.english: I'll call you.
example.fact: 电话 combines 电 ("electricity" — itself a simplified pictograph of a lightning bolt, per this word’s own character notes) with 话 ("speech, words") into a strikingly literal "electric speech," a compound coined when the telephone was still a genuinely new technology needing a brand-new word.

components.note: Depicts a child wrapped in swaddling, related to 子 (child); the picture-meaning has nothing to do with its modern grammatical role marking a completed action or change of state.

example.hanzi: 为了健康,他每天都运动。
example.pinyin: Wèile jiànkāng, tā měitiān dōu yùndòng.
example.english: For the sake of his health, he exercises every day.
example.fact: 为了 typically opens a sentence to state a goal before the main clause describes the action taken to reach it ("为了 + goal, + action") — roughly the mirror image of English, which usually states the action first and tacks the purpose on afterward with "in order to" or "so that."

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — ancient texts were written on bound bamboo strips, and 第 originally referred to the sequential order of such strips, giving rise to its meaning 'ordinal number' (as in 第一, first).
A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dìyī cì lái Zhōngguó.
example.english: This is my first time coming to China.
example.fact: 第 attaches to a number to form an ordinal — pictured, per this word’s own character notes, as bamboo strips (⺮) once used for writing, sorted into sequential order — so 第一 literally frames "first" as "the first [strip] in the sorted stack," the same 第 that marks every ordinal in Chinese (第二, 第三, and so on).

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Bié xiàng tā nàyàng shuōhuà.
example.english: Don't talk like that, the way he does.
example.fact: 那样 mirrors the pilot batch’s 这样 (rank 13) exactly, with the far-demonstrative 那 swapped in for the near 这, and inherits the same manner-vs-degree contrast that entry describes: 那样 describes how something is done, while 那么 (pilot batch, rank 30) more often modifies degree before an adjective.

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.pinyin: Dàjiā hǎo, wǒ jiào Xiǎo Lǐ.
example.english: Hello everyone, my name is Xiao Li.
example.fact: 大家 combines 大 ("big") with 家 ("family, household") into an old image of one big, extended "family" encompassing everyone present. 家’s own character notes trace it to 宀 (a roof) over 豕 (a pig, once a practical marker of a household) — so 大家 quietly carries a household metaphor into its modern, completely general sense of "everyone."

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
二 (two) — 些 originally suggested a small plural amount, building on the idea of 'more than one.'
此 (cǐ) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches the modern reading xiē.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yìxiē shuǐguǒ.
example.english: I bought some fruit.
example.fact: 一些 is built the same way as the pilot batch’s 这些 and this batch’s own 那些 — a demonstrative fused with 些, Mandarin’s built-in small-plural marker — except 一些 drops the demonstrative entirely, using bare "one" to mean an unspecified small quantity rather than pointing at a specific group.

components.note: 田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen bǎ chē tíng zài nàli.
example.english: We parked the car over there.
example.fact: 那里 pairs with the pilot batch’s 这里 (rank 17) as Mandarin’s standard far/near "there"/"here," and like 这里, it has its own casual, erhua-suffixed cousin — 那儿, alongside 这儿 (also in this batch) — giving both demonstratives parallel formal and colloquial forms.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǐwéi nǐ yǐjīng zǒu le.
example.english: I thought you had already left.
example.fact: 以为 carries a strong implication that the belief turned out to be mistaken — 我以为你走了 implies the speaker has just discovered they were wrong — unlike the neutral 认为 (also in this batch) or 觉得 (pilot batch, rank 23), which carry no built-in suggestion of error.

components.note: 高 depicts a tall tower or palace, with a roof at the top and a base below — a simple picture of height.

example.pinyin: Jiàndào nǐ wǒ hěn gāoxìng.
example.english: I'm very happy to meet you.
example.fact: 高兴 typically names an immediate, situational happiness triggered by a specific event ("很高兴认识你," "happy to meet you"), while 开心 and 快乐 lean toward a more general, ongoing good mood or well-wish (as in 生日快乐, "happy birthday") — a distinction English’s all-purpose "happy" doesn’t force speakers to make.

meanings: to be able to take care of

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ néng guòlái bāng wǒ yíxià ma?
example.english: Can you come over and help me for a bit?
example.fact: 过来 completes a trio of "toward the speaker" directional verbs alongside 回来 and 出来 (both also in this batch) — 过 alone contributes "passing across, crossing over," so 过来 pictures someone crossing some distance to arrive at the speaker’s side, while swapping in 去 for 过去 sends them crossing away instead.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 等 pictures bamboo strips, once used as writing tablets, being sorted.
寺 (originally a government office, later 'temple') — sorting and arranging bamboo documents at an official court gave 等 its meanings 'to wait,' 'rank,' and 'etc.'
⺮ (bamboo) — 等 pictures bamboo strips, once used as writing tablets, being sorted.
寺 (originally a government office, later 'temple') — sorting and arranging bamboo documents at an official court gave 等 its meanings 'to wait,' 'rank,' and 'etc.'

example.hanzi: 桌子上有苹果、香蕉等等。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng yǒu píngguǒ, xiāngjiāo děngděng.
example.english: There are apples, bananas, etc. on the table.
example.fact: 等等 is one word doing two unrelated jobs depending on context: reduplicated at the end of a list it trails off into "etcetera," but called out on its own as an interjection it means "wait!, hold on!" — the same character 等 ("to wait") underlies both, just put to very different use in each role.
